code.title: GIL released during waits
code.python:
import threading, time

# Sleeping releases the GIL, so I/O-style waits in threads overlap.
def fake_io(name):
    time.sleep(0.2)          # blocking wait: GIL is released here

start = time.perf_counter()
threads = [threading.Thread(target=fake_io, args=(i,)) for i in range(5)]
for t in threads: t.start()
for t in threads: t.join()
threaded = time.perf_counter() - start

start = time.perf_counter()
for i in range(5): fake_io(i)
serial = time.perf_counter() - start

print("5 waits of 0.2s")
print("serial   >= 1.0s:", serial >= 1.0)
print("threaded <  0.6s:", threaded < 0.6)   # waits overlapped
# Pure-Python CPU work would NOT speed up like this on a GIL build.

followUps:
The GIL is released whenever a thread is about to do something that does not touch Python objects, mainly blocking I/O and long C computations. Examples: time.sleep, socket reads and writes, file reads, lock.acquire, and C libraries such as NumPy, hashlib on large buffers and zlib that explicitly drop it.

It is also taken away from a running thread every switch interval (5 ms by default, sys.getswitchinterval()) so other threads get a turn. Pure Python loops never release it voluntarily, which is why 4 threads summing numbers take about as long as 1.

PEP 703 had to make object bookkeeping safe without one big lock. The main changes: biased reference counting (cheap non-atomic counts for the owning thread plus a shared atomic count for others), immortal objects (never counted), per-object locks on lists, dicts and sets, and a thread-safe allocator (mimalloc) and garbage collector.

Also deferred reference counting for hot objects like functions and modules, and an adaptive interpreter that still specialises bytecode safely. The cost was a single-thread slowdown of roughly 5 to 10 percent in the first builds, and C extensions had to be audited for thread safety.

No. PyPy also has a GIL, so pure-Python threads do not run in parallel there either. PyPy is mainly faster because of its tracing JIT, not because of concurrency.

Jython and IronPython have no GIL because they use the JVM or .NET object model, but they lag behind CPython versions. PyPy has experimented with software transactional memory (PyPy-STM) to remove the GIL, but it is not mainstream. So for CPU parallelism on PyPy you still use processes.

code.title: Concurrency with asyncio.gather
code.python:
import asyncio, time

# Concurrency: three waits overlap on ONE thread (one task runs at a time).
async def fetch(name, delay):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)       # yields to the loop while "waiting"
    return name

async def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    results = await asyncio.gather(fetch("a", 0.2), fetch("b", 0.2), fetch("c", 0.2))
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    print("results:", results)
    print("total about 0.2s, not 0.6s:", elapsed < 0.4)

asyncio.run(main())
# Parallelism would need several cores computing at once, e.g. ProcessPoolExecutor.

followUps:
Yes. Parallelism only needs work to run at the same instant, and it does not require tasks to be interleaved or share a program structure. A single-threaded program that uses SIMD or a GPU kernel, or one process per input file with no coordination, runs in parallel without any concurrent design.

Example: splitting 8 images across 8 independent processes that never talk to each other is parallel, but there is no concurrency to reason about (no shared state, no interleavings). Concurrency is about structure and parallelism is about execution.

Little's law describes concurrency, which is how many things are in flight, not parallelism. It says L = lambda x W: average items in the system equals arrival rate times average time each spends there.

Example: 50 requests per second with 6 seconds average latency means about 50 x 6 = 300 requests in flight, so you need around 300 connections or tasks. Use it to size semaphores, pools and queues, and to see that slow responses silently raise the number you must hold open.

Wrap the sync library in threads and keep a bounded number of them, or find an async alternative. A thread costs 8 MB of virtual address space (stack) and real scheduler work, so 10,000 threads is usually a bad idea, though it can work on a big machine.

Options: (1) use an async driver or HTTP client such as aiohttp or httpx; (2) asyncio.to_thread with a semaphore limiting threads to, say, 100 and queueing the rest; (3) put a proxy or sidecar in front. If most connections sit idle, an event loop with a small thread pool for the sync calls is the compromise.

Free-threading makes threads a real option for CPU-bound Python, because they can run on several cores in one process with shared memory. You avoid pickling costs and the memory of N worker processes.

Trade-offs remain: you now need locks for shared mutable data, some C extensions are not yet ready (the GIL may be re-enabled when they load), and single-thread speed is a few percent lower. Processes still win for isolation and crash containment. asyncio is unchanged for many-connection I/O.

code.title: Race condition and lock fix
code.python:
import threading

balance = 100
lock = threading.Lock()

def deposit_unsafe(barrier, amount):
    global balance
    tmp = balance                 # load
    barrier.wait()                # force both threads to load before either stores
    balance = tmp + amount        # store: overwrites the other deposit

def deposit_safe(amount):
    global balance
    with lock:                    # critical section: load, add, store as one unit
        balance += amount

def run(targets):
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=t) for t in targets]
    for t in ts: t.start()
    for t in ts: t.join()

b = threading.Barrier(2)
run([lambda: deposit_unsafe(b, 10), lambda: deposit_unsafe(b, 10)])
print("unsafe (expected 120):", balance)

balance = 100
run([lambda: deposit_safe(10), lambda: deposit_safe(10)])
print("safe   (expected 120):", balance)

followUps:
Make the read-modify-write one atomic step, then run it many times. For a bank balance: wrap it in a lock, or use a queue so only one thread ever writes.

To catch a rare race, widen the window and repeat: put time.sleep(0) or a Barrier between the load and the store, lower sys.setswitchinterval(1e-6), run 100,000 iterations, and assert the final total (for example 2 x 100000 = 200000). Add stress tests in CI with many threads, use ThreadSanitizer-style tools on free-threaded builds, and log inputs so a failure can be replayed.

sys.setswitchinterval(1e-6)
run_threads(8, increment, 100_000)
assert counter == 8 * 100_000

A race condition is a bug where the outcome depends on timing. A data race is one specific kind: two threads access the same memory at the same time, at least one writes, and there is no synchronisation. They are not the same thing.

You can have a race condition without a data race: two threads each lock correctly to check a balance and then lock again to withdraw, so the check and the act are separate, and both can withdraw from 100 and end at -50. Every access was locked, but the logic is racy. Fix it by holding one lock across check and act.

code.title: Deadlock with timeouts and lock order

followUps:
Livelock is when threads keep running and reacting to each other but make no progress, unlike deadlock where they sit blocked. Picture two people in a corridor who both step aside the same way, again and again.

In code: both threads try for a second lock with a timeout, give up, release their first lock, and retry at the same instant forever. Fix it with randomised backoff (jitter), so one retry lands first, or with a fixed lock order or a single owner of the resource. CPU shows busy while throughput is zero.

Yes. asyncio is single threaded, but coroutines can still wait on each other. If task A holds lock1 and awaits lock2 while task B holds lock2 and awaits lock1, both wait forever even though nothing blocks the thread.

Another form: a task awaits a future that only a blocked loop could complete, or asyncio.Lock is acquired twice by the same task (it is not re-entrant, so the second acquire hangs). The same fixes apply: consistent lock order, asyncio.timeout, and small critical sections.

code.title: Toy event loop: ready queue and timers
code.python:
import heapq
from collections import deque

# A toy event loop: ready queue + timer heap (no real sockets).
ready = deque()
timers = []          # (due_time, seq, callback)
now = 0.0
seq = 0
log = []

def call_soon(cb): ready.append(cb)
def call_later(delay, cb):
    global seq
    seq += 1
    heapq.heappush(timers, (now + delay, seq, cb))

def run():
    global now
    while ready or timers:
        # 1. if nothing ready, jump the clock to the earliest timer
        if not ready and timers:
            now = max(now, timers[0][0])
        # 2. move due timers to the ready queue
        while timers and timers[0][0] <= now:
            ready.append(heapq.heappop(timers)[2])
        # 3. run only the callbacks that were ready at the start of this pass
        for _ in range(len(ready)):
            ready.popleft()()

call_soon(lambda: log.append("t=%.1f first" % now))
call_later(0.5, lambda: log.append("t=%.1f timer 0.5" % now))
call_later(0.2, lambda: (log.append("t=%.1f timer 0.2" % now), call_soon(lambda: log.append("t=%.1f chained" % now))))
call_soon(lambda: log.append("t=%.1f second" % now))
run()
print("\n".join(log))

followUps:
It is implemented as a Future that the loop completes later with a timer. sleep(delay) creates a future, calls loop.call_later(delay, set_result_unless_cancelled, future), and awaits the future. The task then yields that future to the loop and is suspended.

When the timer is due, the loop pops it from the timer heap, runs the callback, which marks the future done, and the future's done-callback schedules the task's step again. sleep(0) is special: it just yields once so other ready tasks run. No thread blocks and no CPU is used while waiting.

Because otherwise a callback that keeps scheduling new callbacks could starve I/O and timers forever. The loop takes a snapshot of the ready count (ntodo = len(ready)) and runs only that many.

Anything scheduled during the pass, such as a task that does await asyncio.sleep(0) in a loop, runs next iteration, after the selector has been polled again. Example: 3 ready callbacks, and the first one adds 2 more. This pass runs 3, the next pass runs 2, and sockets and timers get checked in between.

uvloop replaces the event loop implementation, not asyncio's API. It is a drop-in loop written in Cython on top of libuv, the same C library Node.js uses, in place of the pure-Python selector loop and its transports.

You install it with uvloop.run(main()) or by setting the event loop policy. It typically makes network-heavy code 2 to 4 times faster, mainly by speeding up sockets, streams and callback scheduling. Your coroutines, tasks and futures stay the same. It does not work on Windows.

code.title: gather, TaskGroup and as_completed
code.python:
import asyncio

async def ok(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05 * n)
    return n

async def bad():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    raise ValueError("boom")

async def main():
    # gather with return_exceptions: partial results, nothing cancelled
    r = await asyncio.gather(ok(1), bad(), ok(2), return_exceptions=True)
    print("gather:", [repr(x) for x in r])

    # TaskGroup: a failure cancels siblings, errors arrive as an ExceptionGroup
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tg.create_task(ok(5))
            tg.create_task(bad())
    except* ValueError as eg:
        print("taskgroup caught:", [str(e) for e in eg.exceptions])

    # as_completed: results in finish order
    order = []
    for fut in asyncio.as_completed([ok(3), ok(1), ok(2)]):
        order.append(await fut)
    print("as_completed order:", order)

asyncio.run(main())

followUps:
You keep the task objects and ask them for results yourself, because the group raises one ExceptionGroup and gives you no return value on failure. Create tasks with tg.create_task and read t.result() after the block for those that finished.

Or catch errors inside each child so the group never fails: write async def safe(c): try: return await c; except Exception as e: return e. Then every task succeeds from the group's view and you inspect the returned values, like gather(return_exceptions=True). Without this, one failure cancels the siblings.

except* handles ExceptionGroup, which holds several errors raised together. When a TaskGroup has 3 failing children, you get one group with 3 exceptions. A plain except ValueError cannot match inside a group.

except* ValueError picks out the ValueErrors from the group and runs the handler; the rest stay in a remaining group that keeps propagating. You can write several except* clauses and more than one can run. It was added in Python 3.11 with PEP 654 because concurrent code can fail in several places at once.

try:
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg: ...
except* ValueError as eg:
    print(len(eg.exceptions))

code.title: Task cancellation and timeout
code.python:
import asyncio

async def worker():
    try:
        print("worker: started")
        await asyncio.sleep(10)
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("worker: got CancelledError, cleaning up")
        raise                      # re-raise! swallowing it breaks timeouts
    finally:
        print("worker: finally ran")

async def main():
    t = asyncio.create_task(worker())
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
    t.cancel()                     # request cancellation
    try:
        await t                    # always await a cancelled task
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("main: task cancelled =", t.cancelled())

    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.05):   # built on cancellation
            await asyncio.sleep(1)
    except TimeoutError:
        print("main: timeout converted to TimeoutError")

asyncio.run(main())

followUps:
asyncio.shield(aw) protects the inner task from cancellation of the outer await. If you cancel the caller, it gets CancelledError, but the shielded task keeps running in the background.

That is useful for must-finish work such as committing a transaction. The danger is that the inner task is now unowned: nobody awaits its result or its exception, and on shutdown it may be destroyed mid-way or leak. Always keep a reference to the inner task and await it, or handle it in cleanup. Shielding inside wait_for will not make the timeout wait for it.

Because it is a control signal, not an error, and code with except Exception must not swallow it by accident. Since Python 3.8 CancelledError inherits from BaseException rather than Exception.

Before, a generic handler like except Exception: log(e) would catch the cancellation and the task kept running after task.cancel(), so timeouts and shutdown failed. Now such handlers let it pass. If you catch it on purpose to clean up, re-raise it afterwards, as KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit are also BaseExceptions.

code.title: Blocked event loop vs to_thread
code.python:
import asyncio, time

async def lag_probe(samples):
    # Measures how late a 20 ms sleep wakes up = event loop lag.
    worst = 0.0
    for _ in range(samples):
        t = time.perf_counter()
        await asyncio.sleep(0.02)
        worst = max(worst, time.perf_counter() - t - 0.02)
    return worst

async def blocking_handler():
    time.sleep(0.3)                          # BAD: blocks the whole loop

async def threaded_handler():
    await asyncio.to_thread(time.sleep, 0.3) # GOOD: loop stays free

async def main():
    for name, h in (("blocking", blocking_handler), ("to_thread", threaded_handler)):
        probe = asyncio.create_task(lag_probe(5))
        await asyncio.sleep(0.03)
        await h()
        worst = await probe
        print(name, "-> loop lag over 0.2s:", worst > 0.2)

asyncio.run(main())

followUps:
The default thread pool has min(32, os.cpu_count() + 4) workers, so a 4-core machine gets 8 threads and a big machine gets at most 32 (Python 3.13+ uses os.process_cpu_count()). to_thread uses the loop's default executor.

That matters under load: with 8 workers and 100 concurrent 1-second blocking calls, they finish in about 13 rounds, so the last waits ~13 s. Raise it with loop.set_default_executor(ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=100)) or use a dedicated executor per kind of work.

Measure how late a timer fires and alert when it is high. A small task runs await asyncio.sleep(1) in a loop and records actual - expected as a gauge or histogram. On a healthy loop it is under a few ms.

Alert on the p99 or max over a window, for example lag above 100 ms for 5 minutes, and track it next to request latency and in-flight tasks. Set loop.slow_callback_duration in debug mode to log which callbacks run over 100 ms. When it fires, take a py-spy dump of the worker to see what is blocking.

code.title: What can be pickled and its cost
code.python:
import pickle

def square(x):             # top-level: pickled by qualified name only
    return x * x

class Big:
    def __init__(self, n): self.data = list(range(n))

# Functions pickle by reference (tiny); lambdas and nested functions cannot.
print("top-level function size:", len(pickle.dumps(square)), "bytes")
try:
    pickle.dumps(lambda x: x)
except Exception as e:
    print("lambda fails with:", type(e).__name__)

# Arguments are copied in full: big objects cost a lot.
small = pickle.dumps(("file.csv", 0, 1000))
big = pickle.dumps(Big(100_000))
print("send a description:", len(small), "bytes")
print("send the data     :", len(big) > 100_000, "(over 100 KB)")

# A worker initializer would load the heavy data once per process instead.
print("round trip ok:", pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(square))(7))

followUps:
BrokenProcessPool is raised when a worker process dies abruptly, for example from a segfault, os._exit, or the OS killing it for using too much memory. The pool cannot tell which task failed, so it marks itself broken and every pending future fails with it.

Handle it by catching the error, creating a fresh pool, and resubmitting unfinished work (tasks must be idempotent). Reduce the chance by capping memory per task, using max_tasks_per_child (3.11+) to recycle leaky workers, and not calling sys.exit in tasks. Ordinary Python exceptions do not break the pool.

Fork gives the child a copy-on-write view of the parent's memory, so it starts fast and shares big read-only data for free. But Python touches reference counts whenever it reads an object, and that write makes the OS copy the whole 4 KB page.

So a 2 GB list shared by 8 forked workers slowly turns into up to 16 GB as they read it. Fixes: store data in NumPy arrays or shared_memory (no per-element refcounts), load it once per worker in an initializer, or call gc.freeze() before forking to reduce GC page writes.

code.title: Token bucket, retries and idempotency
code.python:
# Simulated clock: token bucket + exponential backoff for an LLM batch job.
class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate, capacity):
        self.rate, self.capacity = rate, capacity
        self.tokens, self.t = capacity, 0.0
    def take(self, now):
        # refill by elapsed time, then spend one token or report the wait
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (now - self.t) * self.rate)
        self.t = now
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return 0.0
        return (1 - self.tokens) / self.rate

bucket = TokenBucket(rate=50, capacity=5)    # 3000/min = 50/s
now, sent = 0.0, []
for doc in range(12):
    wait = bucket.take(now)
    if wait:
        now += wait
        bucket.take(now)
    sent.append(round(now, 2))
print("send times for 12 docs:", sent)
print("1,000,000 docs at 50/s = %.1f hours" % (1_000_000 / 50 / 3600))

done = set()                                  # idempotent: skip finished docs
def call_with_retry(doc, fail_times):
    delay = 1.0
    for attempt in range(5):
        if attempt >= fail_times:
            done.add(doc)
            return attempt + 1
        delay *= 2                            # 2, 4, 8 ... (add jitter in real life)
    return -1
print("attempts for doc 7 that gets two 429s:", call_with_retry(7, 2))
print("doc 7 already done, skip:", 7 in done)

followUps:
Make the work idempotent and record completion in durable storage before and after each call. Key every result by document ID, write it with an upsert (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING), and on startup skip IDs already stored.

You cannot fully stop a double call: if the process dies after the API answered but before the write, that one request is paid again. Limit it by writing results immediately (or in small batches), tracking an in-progress state with a lease, and using the provider's idempotency key where offered. At 1M docs, redoing the in-flight few hundred is cheap.

Use one shared limiter that all machines ask, instead of each machine guessing. Common choices: a Redis token bucket updated with an atomic Lua script, or a small rate-limit service that hands out permits.

Or split the quota statically: 3,000 / 10 = 300 per minute each, which is simple but wastes capacity when one machine is idle. Better is a central queue that workers pull from, so the number of workers does not matter. Always also honour 429 and Retry-After, as the provider's count is the truth, and leave headroom (say 90 percent of the limit).

code.title: Python 3.13/3.14 concurrency features

followUps:
Maybe, but only after testing, since it is officially supported in 3.14 and not the default. I would check three things: do all my C extensions (NumPy, pandas, database drivers) ship free-threaded wheels, or will they turn the GIL back on at import; does my workload gain from threads; and what happens to single-thread speed and memory.

Plan: run the test suite and a load test on a canary, compare throughput and p99 latency, and run stress tests for races, since code that was safe only by luck under the GIL may now break. Keep the GIL build as the rollback.

Sub-interpreters do not share Python objects; they pass data through channels and queues by copying or by shared buffers. Each interpreter has its own modules, globals and GIL, so this is like multiprocessing but inside one process.

In 3.14 concurrent.interpreters offers Queue objects that carry simple types (None, bool, int, float, str, bytes, tuples of those) and a few more, by copy. Large arrays can be shared with the buffer protocol (memoryview). Sending is cheaper than pickling to another process, but you cannot send an arbitrary object or share a list.

code.title: Producer-consumer with sentinels
code.python:
import queue, threading

q = queue.Queue(maxsize=3)         # bounded: put() blocks when full (back-pressure)
SENTINEL = None
N_CONSUMERS = 2
results, lock = [], threading.Lock()

def producer():
    for i in range(10):
        q.put(i)
    for _ in range(N_CONSUMERS):
        q.put(SENTINEL)            # one stop signal per consumer

def consumer():
    while True:
        item = q.get()
        try:
            if item is SENTINEL:
                return
            with lock:
                results.append(item * item)
        finally:
            q.task_done()          # always, even on errors

threads = [threading.Thread(target=consumer) for _ in range(N_CONSUMERS)]
p = threading.Thread(target=producer)
for t in threads: t.start()
p.start()
p.join()
for t in threads: t.join()         # clean shutdown: join every thread
print("input   : 0..9")
print("squares :", sorted(results))

followUps:
Because empty() can change between your check and your get, so a consumer can block forever. Another thread might take the last item right after your empty() returned False, and then get() blocks with nothing left.

It also stops too early: empty() is True while a producer is just about to put, so the consumer quits and the late items are lost. Example: 1 item left, two consumers both see not empty, one gets it, the other hangs. Use a sentinel, q.shutdown() (3.13+), or get(timeout=...) with an Event.

The ideas are the same, but items cross a process boundary, so they must be picklable and are copied. multiprocessing.Queue uses a pipe and a feeder thread, so put returns before the data is really sent, and empty() and qsize() are unreliable (qsize fails on macOS).

Use multiprocessing.JoinableQueue for task_done/join. Send one sentinel per consumer process. Drain the queue before join()ing a producer process, or it can deadlock because the feeder thread has unflushed data. Terminated processes can also corrupt a queue.

code.title: Dumping stuck thread stacks

followUps:
Make the interleaving happen on purpose instead of waiting for luck. Use a threading.Barrier or Events to force the bad order (both threads load before either stores), or inject time.sleep between steps in a test hook.

For general coverage, run the test many times with many threads, shrink the switch interval with sys.setswitchinterval(1e-6), add random delays at suspect points, and assert invariants (for example the total equals the sum of deposits). In asyncio, replace the awaited call with a controlled Future so you decide when it completes. Record the seed so a failure can be repeated.

Only the calling thread exists in the child after fork, but the child gets a copy of the memory, including locks that other threads held at that moment. Those locks are never released in the child, so the child can deadlock on the first use of a logging, malloc or import lock.

Example: thread B holds the logging lock while thread A forks; the child calls logging.info and hangs forever. That is why Python 3.12 warns about fork in a multi-threaded process and 3.14 moved the Linux default to forkserver. Use spawn or forkserver, or fork before starting threads.
